evidence.title: U11: A standard patent takes a median 980 days to grant; a trade mark 223 days to register
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For applications filed FY2010 to FY2019, standard patents took a median 980 days (about 2.7 years) to grant, the middle half 681 to 1,318 days. Trade marks took a median 223 days, with a sharp peak at about 222 days; WIPO gives IP Australia's average time from filing to registration in 2016 as 222 days (U70), so the peak matches the office's usual path.

- 99% of standard patents are granted within 2,156 days; 99% of trade marks within 1,081, with a long tail.
- Designs take a median 33 days and second-tier patents 21; an innovation patent was granted after a check of formalities only, so its 21 days are not compared with standard patents'.
- 57 values remain negative (registered before filed), down from 1,497 before the repairs. They are left as recorded.

evidence.text:

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the IP rights lens)
evidence.text:
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.
3. Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began).
   - _Why:_ 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.
4. Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration".
   - _Why:_ The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.
5. The "technology area" is kept for patents only.
   - _Why:_ For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.
6. An attorney counts only if the agent on record is not the applicant itself.
   - _Why:_ The register's "agent" is the address for service, which is often the applicant's own; counting it said every trade mark had an attorney.

evidence.title: U31: Each right's milestones were added only after five checks of how the register records them
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Eleven columns of milestones (examination, acceptance, opposition, assignment, extension, lifetime) rest on five checks of IP RAPID's event records. Among them: trade marks' recorded ends fall from 3,213 in March 2026 to 0 from May, probably because an end is recorded only after the grace period for renewal, so trade marks and designs are treated as observed only to 31 March 2026.

- **No separate grant column.** A patent's grant event falls on its registration date for 99.99% of granted patents.
- **Assignments counted once.** 99.78% of patents with an assignment have it published twice, as an assignment and as a party change; the first is used.
- **Only standing events.** 4.76% of patent lapse events were later reversed, and 60.47% of the patents with one are now granted, expired or ceased.
- **When a term starts.** 92.19% of ceased trade marks whose two filing dates differ (mostly international ones) end a whole number of years after the earliest; 84.59% of standard patents ceased since 1996 end 6 to 7 months after an anniversary, at the end of the grace period.

evidence.title: U33: Patent examination stretched to 755 days for FY2006's applications and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The median time from a standard patent's examination request to its acceptance rose from 408 days (FY1990) to 755 (FY2006), and has been 422 to 516 days since FY2014. Trade marks went from 666 days to acceptance (FY1990) to 52 to 184 days from FY2005.

- Filing to examination request, standard patents: 192 days (FY2000), 652 (FY2005), 552 (FY2010), 309 (FY2015) and 553 (FY2021). For FY2013 it is 44 days: applicants asked for examination before Raising the Bar took effect, which kept their applications under the old law.
- Certification: 123 to 208 days after grant for innovation patents and 73 to 276 days after registration for designs.
- The latest years are still in progress, so their medians are understated.

evidence.title: B2: The strongest pairs are how the IP system works, not findings, and are recorded but not carried forward
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The strongest leads are what the filing rules and the way records are made would produce anyway. Australian filers file their international (PCT) applications at IP Australia (strength 0.945), and the inventions they file are made here (0.892). A patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination (0.83).

- Each held in the earlier decade too: 0.938, 0.851 and 0.817.
- **The applicant sets part of the pace.** A standard patent's time to grant rises with how long its owner waits before asking for examination; the office is not the only source of delay.
- **A record effect.** Wider families have fewer inventors of unknown country (0.526; 0.582), because Google Patents takes inventors' countries from foreign publications, which narrow families lack (U95).
- **Trade marks:** expedited examination goes with a priority claim (0.78; 0.763), the recording U103 explained.
- **Provisionals:** individuals have no ABN (0.757; 0.738). **Trade marks:** a founding applicant's country goes with its priority office (0.731; 0.774).

evidence.title: B7: Australian organisations' patents took longer to grant than overseas ones in one decade but not the other, so this is not a lead
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text: **B7 (observational). Australian organisations' standard patents took longer to grant than overseas organisations' in FY2010 to FY2019, but not in FY2000 to FY2009: not a lead.** Granted standard patents, median years from application: Australian organisations 3.12 against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years, interval 0.435 to 0.52; rank-biserial 0.179), but 3.41 against 3.32 in FY2000 to FY2009 (0.082, 0.044 to 0.123; 0.016). From the examination request the difference is 0.17 years (0.153 to 0.181) in the later decade and -0.079 (-0.099 to -0.057) in the earlier. The route is the candidate third factor: a PCT application's clock starts at national phase entry, about 30 months after its priority (U6), and overseas filers use the PCT most (section 1.5); the screen ties time to grant to the route (0.304; 0.237: claiming an Australian application, a median 1,617 days).

evidence.title: U5: Standard patent applications held steady over the last ten years, while trade marks and designs rose
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In FY2017 to FY2026 there were 28,798 to 32,960 standard patent applications a year. Trade marks rose from 72,652 (FY2017) to 98,189 (FY2026), designs from 7,727 to 10,388, and plant breeder's rights fell from 413 to 255. Second-tier patents peaked at 7,150 in FY2021, the year innovation patents closed, then fell to 52 (FY2026).

- Provisional applications ran at 4,143 to 5,343 a year in FY2017 to FY2025, then doubled to 10,069 in FY2026 (U8).
- In the chart, standard patents of "origin unknown" give way to "overseas" ones between about 1975 and 1990; from FY1990 at most 0.45% a year are of unknown origin (FY1993). The change is in what the register records, not necessarily in who filed.
- **Corrected.** Before 1983 for trade marks, 1986 for designs and September 1985 for provisional applications, the register holds only the rights still alive when it was computerised, so those early counts understate filings (U23).

evidence.title: U4: Most rights are trade marks, and most patents are standard patents
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Trade marks are 53.6% of all rights, patents 40.22%, designs 5.914% and plant breeder's rights 0.2693%. Of patents, 82.17% are standard patents, 15.07% provisional applications and 2.77% second-tier patents.

- Petty patents run from FY1980 to FY2001 and innovation patents from FY1999; innovation patents still appear in FY2027 as divisionals and conversions of earlier applications.
- Trade marks other than ordinary ones are rare: 3,033 certification, 2,594 collective and 1,456 defensive marks.
- **Decision.** A count of "rights" across types is mostly a count of trade marks, so totals are always given by type, and patent headlines use standard patents.

pool.text:
- **Later standard patents more often stay in force; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years.** Standard patents' median time in force rose from 10.6 years (granted in the 1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). These are shares still on the register, not value; the research owner adopted years in force as a working measure for Stage 2, alongside other signals. Observations: U36.
- **US patents often cite Australian research, and R&D spending has fallen.** US patents often cite Australian research institutions' work; 93.6% of those citations come from patents with no Australian applicant or inventor, as most US patents have none. A citation is not use. Australia's R&D spending rose to 2008 as a share of GDP and has fallen since, below the OECD median. Observations: U85, U65, U66.
- **The register's history shapes what it can say.** Early years hold only the rights that survived until records were computerised; some events were dated in batches; patent ownership history starts in FY2003. Each is handled, but each limits comparisons over time. Observations: U23, U17, U34.

pool.title: U36: Later standard patents are more often still in force at 10 and 15 years; about half of trade marks are still in force after ten years
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For each granted or registered right, take its years in force from grant or registration, and whether it has ended.
2. Group rights into cohorts by the date their term follows.
3. For each cohort, work out the share still in force after each number of years, counting unfinished rights for as long as they have run (a Kaplan–Meier survival curve); readings with fewer than 30 rights still at risk are left blank.
4. Read off the median and the shares in force after 10 and 15 years. A patent ends on the record six months after the anniversary at which it was not renewed, so "after 10 years" means after the ninth anniversary's renewal; a trade mark ends at the anniversary, so "after 10 years" means after the tenth anniversary's renewal fell due.

**Which gives observation U36:** Of standard patents granted in the 1980s, 53.2% were still in force 10 years after their date of patent; of those from the 2000s and 2010s, 67.5% and 67.3%. The median time in force rose from 10.6 years (1980s and 1990s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). For trade marks the share still in force after 10 years fell, from 67.0% of those filed 1983 to 1989 to 46.9% of the 2000s' and 47.5% of the 2010s'.

pool.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (4 reasoning steps)
pool.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. For Australian individuals, find the share of standard patents granted, filed alone and with an attorney.

events.answer:
A standard patent typically took **980 days (about 2.7 years) to be granted**, compared with **223 days for a trade mark to be registered**, in the atlas’s U11 analysis.[1]

These are medians for applications filed in FY2010 to FY2019: the median is the middle wait, with half taking less time and half taking more.[1] The figures cover successful applications only—not those that never reached grant or registration.[2]

The patent wait is not all time spent at the office. B2 found that longer waits before applicants requested examination went together with longer times to grant, so the office is not the only source of delay.[3]

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Divisional applications rose from 11.59% to 22.62% of Australian organisations' standard patents between FY2000 to FY2009 and FY2010 to FY2019, and from 7.08% to 15.63% of overseas organisations'. With the field, co-filers and classes held the rise holds (+10.7 and +8.8 points), it holds without the ten filers with the most divisionals, and it holds within the same filers: +19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones.

- **Australian organisations:** +11.0 raw, +10.7 held together (96.9% left). Without the ten filers with the most later divisionals, +7.1.
- **Overseas organisations:** +8.5 raw, +8.8 held together; without their ten largest +8.4. Their ten largest hold 8.51% of the later divisionals.
- So Stage 2's doubling is not a change in the mix of fields or filers: the same organisations file more divisionals.
- Why is not in the data. Stage 2's lead, that a divisional keeps claims pending longer, needs the dates of each divisional's parent and its examination.

evidence.text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.

evidence.title: U90: Overseas applicants come through the international route; Australians have moved from provisionals to the PCT, divisionals and direct filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The international (PCT) route carried 81.1% of overseas applicants' standard patents in FY2010 and 69.4% in FY2026, while divisionals rose to 19.8%. Among Australian filers, those claiming only an Australian application (usually a provisional) fell from 81.2% (FY1985) to 11.4% (FY2026), and direct filing, claiming nothing, reached 28.3% in FY2026.

- Australians' use of the PCT rose from 7.8% to 45.2% (FY2020) and 34.4% (FY2026); divisionals from 2.0% to 22.5%.
- Overseas applicants claiming a priority abroad without the PCT fell from 81.0% (FY1985) to 10.0%.
- Trade marks: Australians' are 97.9% to 99.2% direct; from overseas, the Madrid system carried 37.9% in FY2005, 57.5% in FY2020 and 44.0% in FY2026.
- Designs from overseas claim a priority abroad for 70.8% (FY1985) to 88.7% (FY2010) and 75.9% (FY2026).

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the IP rights lens)
evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. The ten latest complete years, FY2017 to FY2026, are used.
   - _Why:_ A recent decade describes the system as it is now.
2. Who applied is the filer, the applicants named when the application was filed (its founding applicants). Origin and type are taken from one of them, the first in Australia, or else the first with a known country (ADR 0037).
   - _Why:_ The filer does not change when a right is sold or assigned, and an application with an Australian founding applicant is what IP Australia counts as a resident application.

**Repairs made to the IP rights lens before any observation**

1. Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".
   - _Why:_ Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.
2. Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
   - _Why:_ They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.

pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. One row per ANZSIC division and financial year, FY1990 to FY2026.

**U110 (descriptive). The fees changed on 39 dates (counting each right apart), nearly always upwards; trade marks were cut repeatedly.**

evidence.title: M25: Raising the Bar's rush, and Australians' lower level of patents after it, hold with trend and season held; the Designs Act's step does not stand apart
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Read as an interrupted time series with each series' trend and season held, Raising the Bar (April 2013) brought a rush of Australians' standard patents (0.605 in logs) and a lower level after it (a step of -0.334, about 28% fewer a month), which then recovers; its controls were quiet but for one small series. The Designs Act 2003's step for overseas applicants (June 2004) does not stand apart: Australians' trade marks, a control, stepped too.

- **Raising the Bar:** a slope of +0.089 a year after the step, a lower level that then recovers. **Overseas applicants:** a rush of 0.352, no step detected (-0.047).
- **Its controls:** Australians' designs, rush 0.049 and step -0.077, quiet; plant breeder's rights, rush 0.206, a small and noisy series. Stage 2's reading holds, with the plant breeder's rights' rush as a caution.
- **The Designs Act 2003:** overseas applicants' designs step 0.391; but Australians' designs step too (0.162), and so do Australians' trade marks (0.251), while Australians' standard patents do not (0.036).

evidence.title: U28: Around some policy changes filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses; around others nothing stands out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
In April 2013, the month Raising the Bar took effect, Australians filed 1,044 standard patent applications, 4.41 times their average month in the year before. In August 2021, when the innovation patent closed to new applications, 2,789 second-tier applications came in (4.31 times), then 95.9% fewer a month in the year after. Patent expiries fell 98.4% when the term rose to 20 years.

- **Rushes before a change:** Raising the Bar (Australians 4.41 times their usual month, overseas applicants 2.65 times; in the year after, 34.0% and 7.7% fewer a month) and the innovation patent's closure. Filing also rose after each change was enacted and before it took effect: second-tier applications by 176.4%, Australian standard patents by 45.3%.
- **Steps:** patent expiries (the 20-year term), extensions of term (the 1999 scheme, from 0.08 to 11.17 a month), second-tier applications when the innovation patent replaced the petty patent (+71.5%), and designs under the Designs Act 2003 (overseas applications +40.4%, Australians' +3.4%).

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney.** Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone. Observations: U20, U48.
- **Provisional applications doubled in FY2026.** 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, mostly from individuals but from organisations too, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is in the filings, not the recording. Why is a question for IP Australia. Observations: U8.
- **Around some policy changes, filing shows clear rushes, steps and pauses.** Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.41 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began; around other changes nothing stands out. These timings are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need. Observations: U28, U3.

evidence.title: B37: Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month; most of those breaks were certain by law, and few show applicants' behaviour
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each policy change, the size of the jump or step in the series it targets was compared with the same measure at up to 72 placebo months, five years either side. Seven of the eight changes moved at least one target series further than any placebo month; the Patents Act 1990 did not. Most of these breaks were made certain by the law or the office's processing (no expiries under a longer term, no applications once a right closed). Those that show applicants' behaviour are the rush before Raising the Bar and, perhaps, overseas applicants' step under the Designs Act 2003.

- **Behaviour: Raising the Bar (April 2013).** Australians' and overseas applicants' standard patents both jumped further than in any of 72 placebo months, and Australians' filing stayed lower in the year after. Series it should not have moved (Australians' designs, plant breeder's rights) did not: 37.5% to 81.94% of placebo months moved as much.
- **Behaviour or administration: the Designs Act 2003 (June 2004).** Overseas applicants' designs stepped up further than in any placebo month; Australians' designs did not step beyond the ordinary (61.11% of placebo months as large).

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Policy changes broke series as the law required; few breaks show behaviour, and fee changes rarely moved filing.** Seven of eight policy changes moved a series further than any comparison month, but most of those breaks were certain by law. The rush before Raising the Bar is the clearest sign of applicants' behaviour. Of the changes in fees to obtain a right, only one break went the way a price would; of the changes in renewal fees, only one (trade marks, July 1993) survives every check. Observations: B37, B47, B49.
- **Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer.** From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisional applications, Australian organisations' inventors include more women than Australian individuals'. Observations: B17, B18.
- **Across industries, the patents allocated by technology follow R&D once services are counted.** Industry counts are applications allocated by what they protect, not what each industry's businesses file. Through the crosswalk with services, patents allocated per business follow business R&D per business. A division's share of innovating businesses showed no clear pattern with patenting in three surveys. Observations: B53, B54, B42, B60.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Across countries and industries, patents follow business R&D.** Across OECD members, patenting at home follows business R&D at the same income and size; across industries, patents allocated per business follow business R&D at the same value added. Australia is nearest Norway, New Zealand and Sweden on non-IP indicators. Observations: M17, M18, M22.
- **Institutions: research that patents cite goes with their own patenting; licence income does not follow patents.** Across every kind of institution, with kind and size held, research that patents cite goes with more patents per work. events.answer:
**The evidence strongly supports a rush around Raising the Bar, but it does not yet establish that the reforms caused it.** The rush remains clear after accounting for the usual trend and seasonal filing patterns. [1]

### What the atlas found
Raising the Bar tightened Australia’s patent law from 15 April 2013, and applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules. [2] In the descriptive finding U28, Australians filed 1,044 standard patent applications that April—4.41 times their average month in the year before. [3]

Stage 2’s B37 found that Australian and overseas applicants’ filing jumps were larger than those around any of the comparison months tested. [4] Stage 3’s **M25 confirmed that the rush held up** when trend and season were accounted for; Australians’ filings also shifted to a lower monthly level afterwards, then recovered. [5]

### How sure can we be?
Taken together, the timing, the rush to use the old rules and the later checks make this a strong sign of applicants responding to the reforms—not just an ordinary busy month. [6] But the comparison series were not entirely quiet: plant breeder’s rights also showed a rush in a small, noisy series, which M25 flags as a caution. [7]

So the careful conclusion is **a clear behavioural response consistent with the reforms, rather than a proven causal effect**; the atlas says establishing what happened because of an intervention requires further causal analysis beyond Stage 3. [8]

Applied, it closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to an ABN and changes no firm finding. Adopting it is the owner's decision (OQ26). Observations: M12, U126.

evidence.title: M12: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (2 steps for this observation, on the firms lens)
evidence.text:
**For this observation**

1. The filer's name is matched to the ABR's main names and ASIC's company names (current and former), and a match is kept only if exactly one ABN has the name and is registered in the filer's state (name_matched_abn, ADR 0045 and 0047).
   - _Why:_ A name shared by several ABNs, or found in another state, is too likely to be the wrong firm.
2. The match is tested on rights whose ABN is known, with the ABN hidden.
   - _Why:_ Shows how often the match is right before it is used where the ABN is missing.

**Repairs made to the firms lens before any observation**

1. Applications are credited to the business that filed them, not the one that holds them now.
   - _Why:_ Otherwise a firm's filing record would change whenever it bought or sold rights.
2. The ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP are flagged, and IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
   - _Why:_ IPLORD counts differently from IP RAPID; adding the two would mix measures.

evidence.title: M12: A name match to the business register recovers most missing business numbers accurately, and changes no firm finding
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Run the match on rights with a known ABN, hidden, and measure the share recovered and the share naming another ABN.
2. Run it on rights with no ABN, and read U45's linked shares and first observed filers with and without it.
3. Read U44's concentration and M8's claimants with the matched links beside the counts.

**Which gives observation M12:** Matching Australian organisations' rights that have no filer's ABN to the ABR's and ASIC's names recovers a known ABN for 66% to 85% of rights where the ABN was hidden for a test, with 1.1% to 4.8% of matches naming another ABN. Applied to rights with no ABN it links 17.7% to 35.3% of them. It closes most of the recent fall in standard patents linked to an ABN, and moves concentration and the claimants' figures by less than a point.

evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Check the column is set only for Australian organisations' rights with no filer's ABN.
2. Count what it adds, by kind of right and by firm.

**Which gives observation U126:** The name match finds an ABN for 16.48% of Australian organisations' trade marks with no filer's ABN, and 28.95% of standard patents, but none of the plant breeder's rights. Counted by firm, the matched filings add 2.03% to the standard patents credited by ABN, 2.80% to trade marks and 7.59% to provisionals, concentrated in a few large organisations. They are kept apart, never added to the counts.

evidence.text:
- **Assumption:** An ABN stands for one business. Related companies in the same group have different ABNs and are counted separately.
- **Assumption:** A right with no ABN recorded for its filer cannot be credited to any firm; such rights are left out of firms' counts rather than guessed.
- **Limit:** The table is not a census of Australian businesses. A business found in none of the six sources is not in it, so rates worked out on this table are rates among these firms (U112 shows how much that matters).

evidence.title: Limits and assumptions
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

- **Firms.** Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds; IP RAPID's recent filings carry fewer, and IP Australia's register restores most for trade marks and designs (U41, U45, U100). A name match recovers most of the rest and changes no firm finding, but is kept apart from the counts (M12). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more (U112), the main third factor every firm signal lacks.
- **Industries.** Industries reach patents only through a crosswalk; the recommended one leaves out services, so a second one with services sits beside it (U75, U114).
- **Places.** Places reach IP only through postcodes, and half the universities' patents carry a postcode where no one lives (U49, U87).
- **Institutions.** Research institutions reach their IP through a reviewed list of names and business numbers that someone in the sector has yet to check (U81, OQ11).

section: Open questions for the research owner
evidence.text:
- **Review Stage 3's two tables**: the fifteen early signals and thirteen data gaps above, before the questions are answered.
- **The name match** (OQ26): whether to adopt the matched business numbers into the firms' counts, or keep them beside the counts (M12).
- **A sector check of the institutions link** (OQ11): a half-hour review by someone who knows the sector, which every institutions result rests on (M23, M24, M38).
- **Firms' size and industry for small firms** (OQ20): known only for employers of 100 or more; small firms need a paid or requested source.
- **Older Australian patent families** (OQ21): repair the links from the EPO's patent family service (free, but an account in your name), or read family measures from FY2010 only.
- **Court judgments after March 2025** (OQ22) and ABS TableBuilder (OQ4, on hold).

evidence.title: Lens: Firms
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Every Australian Business Number that appears in IP RAPID, IP Australia's register, IPLORD, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender (government contracts) or the ATO's tax transparency reports, with what the business is, where it is registered, how old it is on the record, the IP it filed and holds, its R&D claims, its large-company income and its contracts. It is the businesses found in those sources, not every business in Australia, so a share of all businesses, or of all large employers, is taken over a wider count (B50). For employers of 100 or more, WGEA's reports add a size band and an industry; smaller firms have neither. Stage 3 added four counts of filings found by matching the filer's name to the business register, read beside the counts by ABN and never added to them (M12, U126).

Unit: One row per business number (ABN). Rows: 463,279 ABNs.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Who has filed.** 325,650 firms (70.29%) have a filing linked, through IP RAPID's filer's ABN or IP Australia's register; 72,265 (15.6%) have another link to IP only (holding a right, or an older IP record); 65,364 (14.11%) have none. No filing linked is not proof that a firm never filed: its ABN may not have been recorded.
- Plotted on log scales, the number of firms filing a given number of applications falls in a near-straight line: a long tail (skew).

evidence.title: U101: More firms had their first observed trade mark in FY2026; most had no earlier link to IP
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
A firm's first observed filing is its earliest application linked to its business number, not necessarily its first ever. Counted by IP RAPID's business numbers, firms with a first observed trade mark fell from 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026. With the register's numbers filled in, they rose: 14,728 in FY2024, 15,818 in FY2025 and 19,730 in FY2026.

- First designs: 414 against 535 filled (FY2024), 342 against 608 (FY2026).
- **Some are not new.** 2.45% to 5.76% of each year's first observed filers already had an earlier trade mark on another record (483 of 19,730 in FY2026), and 4.32% to 9.1% had some earlier link to IP (852 in FY2026). The counts overstate new filers by about that much.
- **And some are missed.** A firm whose first filing carries no business number anywhere is missed, or counted in a later year. So the counts are neither upper nor lower bounds on new filers: both errors are present.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.

evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Match every filer's name and business number against the reviewed list.
2. Count how each right was matched.
3. For each university, work out the share filed through its company.

**Which gives observation U81:** UNSW files 96.5% of its patent applications through NewSouth Innovations, the University of Newcastle 72.8% through Newcastle Innovation and Adelaide 43.9%, while Queensland files 2.1% through UniQuest and Sydney, Monash and QUT under 1%. Without its company, UNSW would show 3.5% of its patents.

events.answer:
Yes—matching firm names can recover missing Australian Business Numbers (ABNs), but it does not find them all and some matches are wrong. Stage 3’s M12 found that adding these links closes most of the recent fall in patents linked to a business number, without changing the firm-level findings. [1]

### How it works
The method checks the filer’s name against main names in the Australian Business Register and current and former company names held by ASIC. It keeps a match only when exactly one ABN has that name in the filer’s state. [2]

### How well does it work?
M12 tested the method by hiding known ABNs and trying to recover them:
- It recovered the known ABN for **66% to 85%** of rights in the test. [3]
- **1.1% to 4.8%** of matches pointed to a different ABN. [3]
- Applied to rights actually missing an ABN, it linked **17.7% to 35.3%** of them. [4]

The extra links barely changed how concentrated firms’ filings were, or the figures for research and development claimants. [5]

### What are the limits?
This is a tested data-linking method, not a complete repair: many missing ABNs remain unresolved, and trading and business names are not yet included. [6] The matched links are currently kept alongside the main counts, not added to them; whether to adopt them is an open decision for the research owner. [7]

evidence.title: B29: Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together, in both halves of the areas
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
For each standard deviation of advantage (the IRSAD score), a postal area files 1.717 times as many standard patents per person (1.857 in the second half; 1.884 with areas pooled into larger SA3s). Inner regional areas file at 0.259 of major cities' rate. Read together, advantage's ratio is 1.442 and inner regional areas still file at 0.382 of the cities' rate at the same advantage (that combined reading was not repeated for SA3s).

- Trade marks 1.648 (1.707; 1.477), designs 1.504, provisionals 1.582. Very remote areas file standard patents at 0.173 of the cities' rate.
- **The shape is not a straight line:** standard patents run 0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people across deciles 1 to 8, then 1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10. Most of the gradient is in the most advantaged fifth of areas; trade marks rise more steadily (7.63 to 29.24).
- The top tenth differs most between the halves (1.62 against 3.37 for standard patents) because its five heaviest filing areas, several of them mostly one firm's patents (U52), fall in the second half. Pooled rates there are fragile; the overall ratio is the steadier reading.

evidence.title: B29: Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together, in both halves of the areas
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Model each type's count on the area's IRSAD score, then on remoteness, then on both.
2. Repeat in the second half and pooled into SA3s.
3. Compare pooled rates by decile of advantage to see the shape.

**Which gives observation B29:** For each standard deviation of advantage (the IRSAD score), a postal area files 1.717 times as many standard patents per person (1.857 in the second half; 1.884 with areas pooled into larger SA3s). Inner regional areas file at 0.259 of major cities' rate. Read together, advantage's ratio is 1.442 and inner regional areas still file at 0.382 of the cities' rate at the same advantage (that combined reading was not repeated for SA3s).

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries; the signals of value disagree.** Filed in the same number of countries, Australian organisations' patents more often stay in force for 10 years than overseas organisations', except those filed only in Australia. But they reach fewer countries and are cited less, mostly because of that reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010. Observations: B8, B11, B12, B55.
- **Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm.** Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer taken out. Areas that gained graduates or income over a decade were not seen to gain filing, so it looks like a standing difference between places. Observations: B29, B30, B58, B59.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Fees look a weak lever.** Owners did not let rights go more often at the anniversary after any of nine renewal fee changes (for patents, within about 1.4 points either way), and with trend and season held most filing fee breaks do not behave as prices would. Observations: M28, M34.
- **Among firms, age, form and size go with filing; R&D spend only weakly.** Older R&D claimants and public companies more often have a filing linked, held together; government suppliers that file win about two and a half times the contracts; among large employers the size gap widens within an industry. Spending above the median goes with a standard patent by only 4 to 5 points. Observations: M8, M9, M11, M29.
- **Places: one advantage gradient, and what lies beyond it.** Advantage, income and education are mostly one measure. Beyond it, business density, manufacturing businesses and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing; residents' incomes add nothing detectable; remoteness stays. Observations: M13, M14, M31, M32.

evidence.title: M14: Beyond advantage and remoteness, business density and places with more degrees than their resources suggest go with filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (3 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Model each kind of filing against the first component (advantage) alone.
2. Add the other three components and remoteness, and read each rate ratio with the others held.
3. Compare the advantage ratio held with alone, on a log scale, and give the outcome.

**Which gives observation M14:** With the four components and remoteness held together, the advantage gradient is still there but weaker: each standard deviation of advantage goes with 1.256 times the standard patent rate, against 1.932 with advantage alone (first half), so 35% to 39% of the raw ratio remains. Two other dimensions go with filing: business density, and degrees and R&D claimants beyond what an area's resources would suggest. Remoteness stays.

evidence.title: What comes next
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **Stage 2, pairs of variables.** When: Complete (28 October 2026; reviewed 2 November) Asks: Which pairs of measures move together, in what shape, how strongly, and for whom? How: Within each lens, every pair of variables was screened on one scale. A pair counted as a lead only if it was at least small, survived the correction for the number of pairs tested, and held in a second period or sample; the planned pairs were then measured in plain units, with intervals. Example: Postal areas with more advantaged residents file 1.7 to 1.9 times as many standard patents per person for each step of advantage, and the gradient is not one firm's (B29, B30). Adds: The first **observational** evidence: associations that bear on who benefits (Q2) and on the conditions for value (Q3), each with its candidate third factors. Done when: Every pair within each lens screened; each lead with its size and interval, past the correction and held in a second sample.

evidence.title: B58: Higher-income areas file more, and individuals there file more for each person who runs a business
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across postal areas (2023-24), taxable income per individual goes with standard patents per 10,000 people at a rank correlation of 0.384 and with trade marks at 0.453. The share of people with business income goes with filing far less (0.145 and 0.194). Individuals' own applications per 1,000 people with business income rise from a median 3.84 in the most disadvantaged tenth of areas to 11.0 in the most advantaged.

- The second half of the areas agrees: 0.405, 0.518, 0.229 and 0.212.
- Individuals' own filing per person in business barely moves with the share running a business (-0.078; -0.14).
- **So** the advantage gradient is not only that advantaged areas have more business owners.

evidence.title: M16: Postal areas do not fall into distinct kinds; one group of 288 advantaged city areas holds more than half the patents
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: For analysts: the notebook's own words
evidence.text:
- **713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- The other three groups (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage (-0.80, -0.30 and -0.80), file 0.37 to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people, and differ on the second and fourth components and in how many of their people live in major cities (49%, 1% and 7%).
- **So** the concentration of filing in a minority of advantaged, educated, city areas is the clearest structure in the places lens; the rest is a continuum.

evidence.title: B58: Higher-income areas file more, and individuals there file more for each person who runs a business
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Step 4 of 4: From the data to the observation (2 reasoning steps)
evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Relate taxable income per individual, and the share with business income, to filing rates, in both halves.
2. Divide individuals' own applications by those with business income, and compare by tenth of advantage.

**Which gives observation B58:** Across postal areas (2023-24), taxable income per individual goes with standard patents per 10,000 people at a rank correlation of 0.384 and with trade marks at 0.453. The share of people with business income goes with filing far less (0.145 and 0.194). Individuals' own applications per 1,000 people with business income rise from a median 3.84 in the most disadvantaged tenth of areas to 11.0 in the most advantaged.

evidence.title: B30: The advantage gradient is not one firm's; it is at least as strong with each area's largest filer taken out
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Each area's largest filer holds 29.2% of the 24,879 Australian standard patents placed in 2,528 areas. Without it, the rate ratio per standard deviation of advantage is 1.897 (interval 1.74 to 2.067), against 1.717 with it; in the second half, 1.961 against 1.857.

- Single large filers (U52) add noise to areas' counts, not the gradient.
- **Approximate.** A patent joins a filer by its first founding applicant with an ABN, which for a jointly filed patent need not be the party whose postcode places it (about one patent in 20 joined to firms is jointly filed, B26), so "each area's largest filer" is approximate.

evidence.title: M16: Postal areas do not fall into distinct kinds; one group of 288 advantaged city areas holds more than half the patents
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Grouping postal areas by their four components gives at most a weak structure: the best grouping, five groups, has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments (0.5 or more). Read as a description, one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas files 3.14 standard patents a year per 10,000 people and holds 13,993 of the 24,879 patents placed (56%); the rest is a continuum.

- Silhouettes for two to eight groups run from 0.232 to 0.269.
- **288 areas** (4,451,909 residents; 95% of their people in major cities; median IRSAD 1,088), high on advantage (1.36) and low on the third component (more degrees and R&D claimants than their resources): 50.13 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- **713 areas** (11,871,712 residents, the most), above average on advantage (0.78): 0.59 patents and 13.37 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.
- **The other three groups** (260, 539 and 725 areas) are below average on advantage and file 0.37 to 0.48 patents and 8.76 to 10.63 trade marks a year per 10,000 people.

evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
section: Early signals that warrant further investigation

- **Among R&D claimants, older firms, higher spenders and public companies more often have a standard patent linked, held together; among suppliers, company form, age and a city address (not the postcode's advantage); suppliers that file win more contracts and value; among large employers the size gap widens within industry; large taxpayers that file report no more income.** Observations: B22, B23, B24, B50, B51, M8, M9, M11, M12, M29. evidence.text:
The steps are not findings; only the last is.

1. Measure how far each characteristic can be predicted from the others (variance inflation).

section: Step 3 of 4: How it was prepared (1 step for this observation, on the places lens)
pool.text:
**For this observation**

1. Australian standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026, placed by the filer's postcode, with the largest filer in each area taken by the filer's party, whether or not it has an ABN.
   - _Why:_ The same party that gives the patent its postcode, as the final review asked.

**Repairs made to the places lens before any observation**

1. Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
   - _Why:_ A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.
2. A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
   - _Why:_ A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.
3. Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
   - _Why:_ So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.
4. Values published for other kinds of area are moved to postal areas by their 2021 residents.
   - _Why:_ A count can be split by where people live; a median or rate is averaged, weighted by the people shared.

pool.text:
Besides testing signals, Stage 3 asked which measures repeat each other and whether there are distinct kinds of place or country. These are descriptive.

- **Places' characteristics are mostly one advantage gradient.** Across 2,525 postal areas the first component, advantage, carries 49.5% of the variation, and IRSAD can be predicted almost entirely from the other measures. No single measure (income, education) should be read as the one that matters. Observations: M13.
- **Places form a continuum, not kinds.** The best grouping of areas has a silhouette of 0.269, short of clear segments; one group of 288 advantaged, educated city areas holds 56% of the placed standard patents. Observations: M16.

pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
18 changes of 10% or more in the cost of obtaining a right (12 rises, 6 cuts) were set against placebo months: 34 pairs of a change and a filing series. Five moved filing beyond 95% of their placebo months (three rushes and two steps), against about 1.7 of each expected by chance. Only one of the five moved the way a price would: Australians' designs fell after the rise of July 1988. The clearest breaks came with new Acts, the Trade Marks Act 1995 and the Designs Act 2003.

- **How a price would push:** filing brought forward before a rise and lower after it; before a cut, filing would wait, and rise after it.
- **The Trade Marks Act 1995** (January 1996): filing by Australians and overseas applicants fell before the rise (2.778% of placebo months as large), which is the Act's pause (B37), not a price.
- **Overseas applicants' standard patents** were filed early before the 15.31% cut of January 1998 (2.778%), the opposite of what a price would do.
- **The Designs Act 2003** (June 2004, a design's filing fee up 122.2%): overseas applicants' designs stepped up (none of 72 placebo months as large), against a price; that is the Act (B37).

pool.title: B23: More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of R&D claimants have no IP filing linked to their business number, at any level of spend
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
Among 17,514 active R&D claimants, 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth have filed a standard patent, rising to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth. The rank correlation between spend and patent applications is only 0.120. 52% of the lowest spenders and 43.1% of the highest have no IP filing linked to their business number.

- The lowest tenth spends a median $44,790 a year; the highest $3.79m.
- **No filing linked** is most common among claimants under 3 years old on the record (72.9%) and least among those 20 years or more (32.6%); more common in private companies (49.2%) than public ones (36.2%), and in outer regional areas (60.3%) than major cities (48%). It does not rise or fall in step with the postcode's advantage.
- **Who they are, together:** 55.3% of the 8,444 are private companies 3 to 10 years old on the record; only 2.4% are under 3.
- **Another link to IP explains little of it:** of the claimants with no filing linked, 10.9% of those 20 years or more, and 4.1% of those under 3, are linked to IP another way (holding a right, another IP record, or an older IP Australia dataset).

evidence.title: M40: Asking for examination before being directed goes with patents more likely to end, not less, against IP Australia's commissioned study
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
IP Australia's commissioned study counts a request for examination made before the Commissioner directs one as a way of speeding examination up, and reports that applicants who speed up are more likely to renew their patents. Built from the open data, the same measure covers 41.39% of granted patents (the study: 41.9%). But with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant, in both periods (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383).

- **The measure reproduces the study's share:** 303,486 standard patents with a date of patent in 2004 to 2016, divisionals left out, of which 191,477 granted; 41.28% were never directed. The share rose between the periods: overseas organisations 0.273 to 0.5148, Australian organisations 0.2357 to 0.4602.
- **By filer, held together:** overseas organisations 1.282, then 1.388; overseas individuals 1.298, then 1.340; Australian organisations 1.005 (not detected either way), then 1.587; Australian individuals 1.169 (not detected once held), then 1.486.

evidence.title: M40: Asking for examination before being directed goes with patents more likely to end, not less, against IP Australia's commissioned study

evidence.text:
- **Why it may differ from the study:** its outcome ("the lifetime over which the applicant renews the patent") and its controls are not in IP Australia's report. Here each patent is followed from its grant, so the comparison is among patents alive at the same age.
- **One reading, to test:** applicants who wait use the years to drop weak applications before grant, the study's own point about delay as an option, so the granted patents of those who were directed are already filtered.

evidence.title: Checked against IP Australia
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **M40: Disputed in part.** Evidence: Added with A36 (section 11.8). The commissioned study (ipr-2025 p9, p10, p13): applicants who speed up examination, including by asking for it early and unprompted (41.9% of granted patents), are more likely to renew, commercialise and build on their patents. The lens reproduces the measure (41.39%, section 11.2), but with the filer, field, route, cohort, co-filers, classes and expedited examination held, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383) What follows: The study's outcome and model are not in IP Australia's report, so this disputes its direction on its own measure, not its model; a question proposed for IP Australia (OQ28) Note: Disputed in part. IP Australia's commissioned study's measure is reproduced (41.39% of granted patents asked for examination before any direction, against its 41.9%), but those patents are more likely to end, not less, with who filed, the field and the route held (1.276 and 1.383). The study's own model is not published, so it is its direction on its measure that is disputed.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
- **Asking for examination sooner is not a sign of a longer life.** Expedited examination's link with staying in force does not survive the filer, field and route held together, and Australian individuals' expedited patents are about a quarter more likely to end in a given year. On the wider measure IP Australia's commissioned study uses, a request made before any direction (41.39% of granted patents), patents are more likely to end, held together (1.276 and 1.383), against the study's finding. Observations: M5, M40.
- **Some Australian invention ends up owned overseas, by two routes.** Granted Australian-founded patents are more often now held only overseas, at the same reach and filer type, and so are patents filed before the firm's first registration. Inventions made here and filed from overseas come in about equal numbers from international teams and from all-Australian ones. Observations: M6, M27, M30.
- **The same organisations file more divisionals.** Divisionals doubled within the same filers (+19.18 points for Australian organisations, +10.97 for overseas ones), not through a change in fields or filers. Observations: M26.

events.answer:
**M40 found that patents whose applicants requested examination before being directed were more likely to end after grant—not stay in force longer.** That runs against the direction reported by IP Australia’s commissioned study, using the same measure of requesting examination early. [1]

### What lies behind it
The atlas closely reproduced how common these early requests were: **41.39%** of granted patents, compared with the study’s **41.9%**. [2] But the link with patents ending remained in both periods examined, after accounting for differences in applicants, technology fields, filing routes, cohorts and expedited examination. [3]

### How much weight to put on it
This is an association, not evidence that requesting examination early makes a patent end sooner. One possible explanation—not a tested finding—is that applicants who wait have more time to drop weak applications before grant, leaving a more selected group of granted patents. [4]

The comparison also has a limit: the commissioned study’s precise renewal-lifetime measure and model are not available in IP Australia’s report. M40 therefore challenges the **direction of the reported relationship**, rather than reproducing and disproving the study’s model. [5] The atlas follows patents from grant, comparing those still in force at the same age. [6]

claims.text: M40 found that patents whose applicants requested examination before being directed were more likely to end after grant—not stay in force longer. That runs against the direction reported by IP Australia’s commissioned study, using the same measure of requesting examination early.

citations.quote: Early, unprompted requests for examination go with patents more likely to end, not less: the open data do not repeat the link IP Australia's commissioned study reports, on the study's own measure, in either period, with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together.** Added at the owner's decision (OQ27, A36).

claims.text: The atlas closely reproduced how common these early requests were: 41.39% of granted patents, compared with the study’s 41.9%.

citations.quote: | 41.39% | of granted standard patents, 2004 to 2016, asked for examination before any direction (the study, 41.9%) |

claims.text: But the link with patents ending remained in both periods examined, after accounting for differences in applicants, technology fields, filing routes, cohorts and expedited examination.

citations.quote: But with the filer, field, route, cohort and expedited examination held together, those patents are more likely to end in a given year after grant, in both periods (hazard ratios 1.276 and 1.383).

claims.text: This is an association, not evidence that requesting examination early makes a patent end sooner. One possible explanation—not a tested finding—is that applicants who wait have more time to drop weak applications before grant, leaving a more selected group of granted patents.

citations.quote: - **One reading, to test:** applicants who wait use the years to drop weak applications before grant, the study's own point about delay as an option, so the granted patents of those who were directed are already filtered.

claims.text: The comparison also has a limit: the commissioned study’s precise renewal-lifetime measure and model are not available in IP Australia’s report. M40 therefore challenges the direction of the reported relationship, rather than reproducing and disproving the study’s model.

evidence.title: B6: Patents that Australian individuals file without an attorney are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Of the standard patents Australian individuals filed alone in FY2010 to FY2019, 4.8% were granted, against 40.6% of those filed with an attorney: a gap of 35.8 points (interval 33.9 to 37.5). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.8 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.4 points).

- **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.2% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.
- **Australian organisations do not show it in both decades:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.0 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,149 applications organisations filed alone were granted 62.1% of the time. Those earlier lone filers may have been firms with their own patent staff; the data do not say.
- **Trade marks show it in both decades, for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points.

- **Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent recorded at any time, so an application dropped early may never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards); and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.

evidence.title: What Stage 3 found
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Every Stage 3 page follows the same five steps, and shows the first three at its top as a chain: what Stage 2 found, what was held together, and what is left.

- **Start from a Stage 2 signal.** Signal. Sub-questions: A pair that held in two samples. A pair of measures that went together in Stage 2, in a first sample and again in a second: for example, filing without an attorney and fewer grants (B6).
- **Name its third factors.** Third factors. Sub-questions: What else could explain it. Stage 2 named, for each signal, the other factors that could make the two measures go together: the route of filing, the year, the field, the filer's type, a place's advantage.
- **Hold them together.** Held. Sub-questions: One model, every factor at once. One model holds every named factor fixed at once, so the signal is read among rights, firms or places alike in all of them. Intervals allow a filer's many rights to be alike, or resample neighbouring quarters in blocks.
- **Compare raw and held.** Compare. Sub-questions: How much of the signal is left. The raw figure (Stage 2's comparison, with nothing held) is set beside the held one. The charts show both: grey for raw, blue for held, each with its 95% interval.

evidence.title: What comes next
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **Stage 3, many variables together.** When: First pass done (3 November 2026); tables await the owner's review. Asks: Do the signals survive once other factors are held together? What structure and groups exist? How: Each signal Stage 2 carried was modelled with its named third factors held together, and its raw and held figures compared (holds, weakened, not detected once held, reversed). The methods the final review asked for were used throughout: intervals that allow a filer's rights to be alike, block resampling of quarterly changes, citations counted at a fixed age, industry comparisons through the crosswalk with services, and research spend as a base. Places' and countries' characteristics were reduced to a few components, and places grouped to see whether they form kinds. Example: Is an area's patent rate still linked to advantage once its business mix and education are allowed for? Yes, but weaker: 35% to 39% of the ratio is left, and business density and degrees beyond resources matter too (M14). Adds: Separates signals that hold from ones explained by something else, and produces two tables: fifteen early signals, with their evidence and strength, and thirteen data gaps, with possible sources and costs. Done when: When the owner has reviewed the two tables and decided on the name match (OQ26).

evidence.title: U8: Provisional applications doubled in FY2026, mostly from individuals but from organisations too
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
FY2026 had 10,069 provisional applications, against 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. In 5,510 the first applicant named at filing was an individual, against 1,413 to 1,986 a year before; in 4,558 it was an organisation, against 2,751 (FY2024) and 3,060 (FY2025). The rise began in early 2025, peaked in March and April 2026, and had eased by September 2026.

- **When.** 345 in March 2024, 481 in March 2025, 1,274 in March 2026 and 1,231 in April 2026, then 750 by September 2026, still about twice March 2024's level.
- **Broad.** Individuals who filed a single provisional rose from 1,538 (FY2025) to 2,507 (FY2026).
- **And concentrated.** 54 individuals filed 10 or more each (1,528 between them), against 9 who filed 183 in FY2025; one filed 375. 45 organisations filed 10 or more (1,258), against 24 (566).

**Held together (raw and adjusted).** A comparison made inside one model with several third factors at once, so that each is held fixed while the others are too. The raw figure is the plain comparison Stage 2 made, with nothing held; the difference between the two is how much of the raw figure those factors account for.

Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive.

pool.title: What Stage 3 found
pool.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
pool.text:
What Stage 3 found

Stage 3 took each signal Stage 2 carried forward and held its named third factors together in one model, to see how much of it is left. The bar counts every check by its outcome; the list gives the findings most worth knowing. All are associations or descriptions, not causes.

Stage 2 found pairs of measures that move together and named, for each, the other factors that might explain it. Stage 3 holds those factors together, signal by signal, and says how much of each is left. It also asks what structure there is among places, countries, industries and institutions. This page sets out how the test works, what its outcomes mean, and every check it made, each linked to its page.

**Held is not controlled.** Holding measured factors fixed is not an experiment: factors the data do not hold can still explain an association, and some associations run backwards. Every Stage 3 finding is observational or descriptive, and none answers a research question yet. Its two tables, early signals and data gaps, await the research owner's review.

**U8 says provisional patent applications surged in FY2026, mostly through individuals, although organisations filed more too.** There were 10,069 applications, compared with 4,143 to 5,047 a year in FY2022 to FY2025. [1]

### What was behind the rise?
It was both broad-based and concentrated: more individuals filed a single provisional, while a small group filed many applications each. [2] Organisations also contributed, with 4,558 applications, up from 3,060 in FY2025. [3]

The rise began in early 2025, peaked in March and April 2026, and had eased by September 2026. [4]

### What does it mean?
**More filings do not necessarily mean more applications being taken further.** Stage 3’s M35 found that individuals’ FY2025 provisionals were followed by a complete application within 12 months less often than in earlier years. [5] That fall remained when the analysis accounted for filing patterns and applicants’ backgrounds, but was not detected among individuals who had also filed in the earlier years; it was concentrated in new and heavy filers. [6]

That follow-up finding concerns FY2025, not the full FY2026 surge, and late recording or use of the international Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) route remain unresolved explanations. [7]

The simplest takeaway is: **provisional filing rose sharply, but the data do not yet explain why or establish what became of those extra filings.** Possible explanations such as new filing channels, costs or drafting tools were not tested in U8. [8]

evidence.title: Overview: what Australia's IP data show so far
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text: - **Institutions whose research US patents cite more also patent more.** Larger, more cited universities file more patents per work. Across institutions, disclosures go with patents and patents with licence income, partly because every measure is divided by the same research spend. No association was detected between industry-partnered grants and joint filing, though a moderate one is not ruled out. Observations: B44, B45, B62.

evidence.title: B44: Across research institutions the kind of institution sorts most measures, and research that patents cite goes with the institution's own patenting
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across 112 institutions with 100 or more works (2017 to 2023), universities win far more ARC grants per 1,000 works than medical research institutes, which have the most citations from US patents per work. The share of an institution's works cited by US patents rises with its own provisionals per 1,000 works (0.583) and with the citations its works receive (0.529).

- 43 universities, 42 medical research institutes and 11 public research agencies.
- NHMRC grants per work go with standard patents per work (0.338; 0.367). Larger institutions win more ARC grants per work (0.803) and file somewhat more standard patents per work (0.269).
- 10.98% of the institutions' patents are filed with another research institution, against 3.5% of their trade marks.
- **A rule, not performance:** universities' far higher ARC grants per work follow from the ARC's rules (universities hold all ARC funding, U83), and larger institutions' higher ARC grants per work are largely universities against medical research institutes.
- The earlier period is mostly the same institutions seven years earlier: a stability check, not a replication.

evidence.title: B45: Larger, more cited universities file more patents per work; industry-partner grants were not seen to go with joint filing
evidence.licence: MIT for the code. The content is the project's own analysis; it quotes public data under each source's licence, as the atlas's data page lists them.
evidence.text:
Across 43 universities (2017 to 2023), size goes with patents per 1,000 works at a rank correlation of 0.743, the share of works cited by US patents at 0.632 and ARC grants per work at 0.637. For the share of ARC grants with industry partners against the share of patents filed with others, no association was detected (0.127, then -0.074), though the intervals reach 0.50 and 0.43, so a moderate link is not ruled out.

- The earlier period agrees: 0.732, 0.759 and 0.628. Citations per work 0.417 and 0.619.
- **As changes** between the periods (42 universities), growth in works goes with the change in patents per work at only 0.111, with no interval. That the levels' links are about which universities are research-intensive, not what changes within them, is a hypothesis.
- Third factors: research intensity, medical schools, and the commercialisation companies that file for the largest universities (U81).
